main_damage_causes: Loss of domestic warmth and nurturing competence in early scenes reduces Hagrid from a fully realised caregiver to a plot-delivery mechanism

Removal of the Paddington farewell and the hospital wing guilt scene strips the Hagrid-Harry relationship of its two most emotionally complex moments, leaving the friendship feeling functional rather than deeply personal

Omission of Hagrid's explicit moral voice on blood purity and Muggle-borns (the Malfoy boy encounter, the defence of Lily) removes him as an active thematic presence on the saga's central prejudice theme
Loss of Hagrid's extended humor, wit, and subversive warmth in the cabin scene (slug visit) — the film reduces him to a functional expository presence rather than a richly characterized friend

Cutting of the post-diary-vision corridor encounter removes the most emotionally layered moment of Harry's conflicted feelings about Hagrid, losing a humanizing beat at Hagrid's most vulnerable narrative point

damaging_scenes.scene: Philosopher's Stone - Hagrid arrives at the hut on the rock (Film Scene 2)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Hagrid does not speak to or address Dudley at all upon entering beyond telling him to 'budge up.' He makes tea, cooks sausages, and settles in with genuine warmth and domestic competence. He also explicitly confronts Vernon and Petunia with sustained moral outrage about what they have done to Harry, culminating in the famous thundering speech about knowing what Harry's letters said.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film compresses Hagrid's entrance and removes almost all of his initial domestic warmth and self-sufficiency. The cooking of sausages, making of tea, and the extended settling-in that establishes Hagrid as a capable, nurturing presence are cut. The film goes almost immediately to the letter reveal.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's opening Hagrid scene meticulously establishes him as warm, competent, and at ease in his own skin — he fills the hut with fire, food, and comfort. Stripping this reduces him to a plot-delivery vehicle and weakens the first impression of his nurturing character, which is foundational to his role as Harry's first genuine caregiver figure.

damaging_scenes.scene: Philosopher's Stone - Hagrid's confrontation with the Dursleys at the hut (Film Scene 2-3)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Hagrid's anger at the Dursleys is extended, morally articulate, and deeply felt. He thunders 'ALL WHAT?' leaping to his feet and filling the room, delivers a sustained furious indictment ('Do you mean ter tell me this boy knows nothin' about ANYTHING?'), and directly confronts Vernon about the letter Dumbledore left. He also explicitly tells them 'Ah, go boil yer heads, both of yeh' — dismissive, confident, and fearless. His anger is on Harry's behalf and rooted in genuine love.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film retains some of Hagrid's outrage (the car crash line, the umbrella threat) but significantly truncates the moral confrontation. The extended shaming of the Dursleys for their deliberate concealment is compressed. Hagrid's line 'go boil yer heads' and the sustained moral indictment disappear, softening his ferocity as Harry's defender.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Hagrid is fearlessly, righteously angry in a way that defines his protectiveness of Harry. The film preserves the shape of the scene but reduces the moral voltage of his defence, making him slightly less the principled champion the book establishes him as.

damaging_scenes.scene: Philosopher's Stone - Hagrid gives Harry the pig tail (Film Scene 3)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Hagrid intends to turn Dudley into a full pig and is rueful that it only partially worked ('Meant ter turn him into a pig, but I suppose he was so much like a pig anyway there wasn't much left ter do'). The self-deprecating humour and admission of imprecision are essential to his character — he acknowledges his limits with good-natured embarrassment.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film keeps the pig tail gag but removes Hagrid's rueful, self-deprecating commentary about intending to turn Dudley into a pig and falling short. The moment plays as pure comic triumph rather than the charmingly imprecise magic attempt it is in the book.
damaging_scenes.explanation: A small but telling loss: the book's version reveals Hagrid's endearing self-awareness about his own limitations. The film turns it into a punchline, losing the nuance that makes Hagrid's character more dimensional — he is powerful but fallible and knows it.

damaging_scenes.scene: Philosopher's Stone - Hagrid's explanation of his expulsion (Film Scene 3)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, when Harry asks why Hagrid is not supposed to do magic, Hagrid openly admits he was expelled from Hogwarts in his third year, that his wand was snapped in half, and that Dumbledore let him stay on as gamekeeper. He is candid, slightly embarrassed, and the exchange closes with his warm praise of Dumbledore ('Great man, Dumbledore'). He also hints — by gripping his umbrella very tightly when Ollivander asks if he still uses the wand pieces — that he does still channel magic through it.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film omits Harry's direct question about why Hagrid cannot do magic and Hagrid's admission about being expelled. Hagrid simply says 'strictly speaking I'm not allowed ter do magic' without any backstory. The Ollivander scene where Hagrid's secret about the broken wand is delicately hinted at is also absent as a beat of Hagrid's characterisation.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Hagrid's expulsion backstory is a defining character detail: it explains his status, his loyalty to Dumbledore, and the hidden sadness of a wizard denied his full nature. Removing the explicit disclosure (and the Ollivander hint) means film audiences never understand this foundational aspect of who Hagrid is and what he has sacrificed.

damaging_scenes.scene: Philosopher's Stone - Diagon Alley: Hagrid and Harry on the Underground (Excluded/Cut scene)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Hagrid's delight at Muggle technology, his complaint about Underground seats being too small, his inability to manage Muggle money, and his wonder at ordinary things ('See that, Harry? Things these Muggles dream up, eh?') all establish his childlike curiosity about the non-magical world and his fish-out-of-water comic charm.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This material was cut from the theatrical release. The film moves directly from leaving the Dursleys to arriving in Diagon Alley, eliminating the entire journey through London. Hagrid's interaction with Muggle infrastructure and his warm, bumbling wonder are entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Underground sequence in the book is a rich vein of Hagrid characterisation — his wonder, his incompetence with Muggle systems, his pride in the wizarding world — all delivered with warmth and humour. Its absence (confirmed as a cut scene) reduces the Diagon Alley trip to a functional errand rather than a character-building journey, diminishing Hagrid's presence as Harry's guide and companion.

damaging_scenes.scene: Philosopher's Stone - Leaky Cauldron: Hagrid explains Quirrell's nervousness (Film Scene 4)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, after meeting Quirrell, Hagrid gives Harry a detailed, warm, and slightly gossipy account of Quirrell's history: brilliant mind, took a year off for firsthand experience, met vampires in the Black Forest, had trouble with a hag, 'never been the same since.' This shows Hagrid as informed, empathetic, and socially embedded in the wizarding world.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has no equivalent explanation from Hagrid about Quirrell's background. Hagrid simply introduces Quirrell and moves on.
damaging_scenes.explanation: A minor but characteristic moment is lost: Hagrid as a knowledgeable, gossipy insider who contextualises the wizarding world for Harry. It also adds ironic depth to the Quirrell mystery. Its absence is a small reduction in Hagrid's voice and social intelligence.

damaging_scenes.scene: Philosopher's Stone - Diagon Alley: Malfoy boy encounter and Hagrid's response (Film Scene 4 area / not depicted)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Harry meets a pale drawling boy (implicitly Malfoy) at Madam Malkin's while Hagrid stands outside eating ice cream and waving. Harry is troubled by the boy's remarks about Muggle-borns not belonging. When Harry tells Hagrid, Hagrid explicitly defends Muggle-born witches and wizards, citing Harry's own mother as a great example: 'Yer not from a Muggle family... some o' the best I ever saw were the only ones with magic in 'em in a long line o' Muggles -- look at yer mum!'
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This exchange — Hagrid waiting outside, Harry's conversation with the Malfoy boy, and Hagrid's subsequent defence of Muggle-borns — does not appear in the film corpus. The scene at Madam Malkin's is cut entirely.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Hagrid's spontaneous, heartfelt defence of Muggle-born wizards, specifically invoking Lily Potter, is both a character-defining moment of his values and an early establishment of the saga's central anti-prejudice theme. Its absence removes Hagrid as a moral voice on blood purity, a role he uniquely fills in this introductory sequence.

damaging_scenes.scene: Philosopher's Stone - Diagon Alley: Hagrid's pride about Dumbledore's trust (Film Scene 6-7)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Hagrid explicitly and proudly tells Harry about the Gringotts errand: 'He usually gets me ter do important stuff fer him. Fetchin' you -- gettin' things from Gringotts -- knows he can trust me, see.' This is a key beat of Hagrid's self-worth and his relationship with Dumbledore.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has Hagrid say the vault errand is 'Hogwarts business, very secret' but does not include the explicit statement of pride about Dumbledore consistently trusting him with important tasks. The emotional beat of Hagrid's dignity and self-esteem tied to Dumbledore's trust is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: A small but meaningful character beat is lost: Hagrid's genuine pride in being trusted, which contextualises his later devastation when he accidentally betrays that trust. The book carefully seeds this pride to make the later guilt more poignant.

damaging_scenes.scene: Philosopher's Stone - King's Cross station farewell (Film Scene 11)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Hagrid helps Harry onto the train, hands him his ticket, tells him to send a letter with Hedwig if there are problems with the Dursleys, and says 'See yeh soon, Harry.' Harry watches him until he is out of sight. Hagrid also buys Harry a hamburger and sits with him beforehand, giving him reassurance: 'Don' you worry, Harry. You'll learn fast enough... Just be yerself... You'll have a great time at Hogwarts -- I did -- still do.' This is a warm, extended farewell that cements the bond.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has a brief farewell at King's Cross. Hagrid gives Harry his ticket, tells him to stick to it, mentions Dumbledore needs him, and leaves quickly. The reassuring conversation, the hamburger, and the extended emotional farewell are absent. Hagrid essentially disappears mid-scene.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's King's Cross farewell is the culminating scene of the foundational Hagrid-Harry bond established in the first act. Hagrid's personal reassurance ('Just be yerself') and the warmth of the parting establish the emotional anchor of their relationship before Harry enters Hogwarts alone. The film's abrupt departure weakens this bond's emotional establishment significantly.

damaging_scenes.scene: Philosopher's Stone - Hagrid's hut: first tea visit with Harry and Ron (Film not depicted in corpus)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Hagrid invites Harry for tea in a personal note, showing ongoing care. The visit establishes his home (hams, kettle, patchwork quilt), his hospitality (rock cakes, tea), his friendship with Ron, his gentle deflection on Snape ('Rubbish! Why should he?'), his knowledge of Charlie Weasley, and Harry's discovery of the Gringotts break-in connection. Critically, it shows Hagrid's subtle discomfort when Harry notices he doesn't quite meet his eyes about Snape.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The first personal tea visit to Hagrid's hut does not appear in the film. The relationship development between Harry and Hagrid as ongoing friends at Hogwarts, outside of plot-functional scenes, is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This scene is foundational to the Hagrid-Harry friendship at Hogwarts. It shows Hagrid as Harry's first social call, his nurturing presence in Harry's new life, and his complex position knowing things he cannot say. Without it, Hagrid's role at Hogwarts is almost entirely plot-functional rather than relationally warm, damaging the friendship's emotional texture.

damaging_scenes.scene: Philosopher's Stone - Quidditch match: Hagrid's defence of Snape in the stands (Film Scene 18)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Hagrid is sitting in the stands with binoculars and is fully integrated into the social scene. He interacts with Ron and Hermione, comments on the game, and is present for the broom crisis. His 'Rubbish! Why would Snape do somethin' like that?' is delivered from a position of personal knowledge and loyalty, not just defensiveness.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film shows Hagrid watching from the stands but his role is reduced. His dialogue defending Snape is present ('Nonsense! Why would Snape put a curse on Harry's broom?') but the warm, socially embedded presence — sitting with the students, having watched from his hut with binoculars before joining — is simplified. His defence of Snape is retained but the warmth of his integration is compressed.
damaging_scenes.explanation: A minor compression: the book's detail of Hagrid watching from his hut first, then joining, and his fuller social integration with the students is simplified. The core beat (defending Snape) is retained, limiting the damage.

damaging_scenes.scene: Philosopher's Stone - Hagrid's hut: dragon egg revelation and Norbert subplot (Film Scene 20)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, the Norbert subplot includes Hagrid's extended, almost delusional attachment to the dragon ('He really knows me now, watch. Norbert! Norbert! Where's Mommy?'), his inability to see the danger ('Shouldn'ta lost me temper... just playing, he's only a baby'), packing a teddy bear, crying 'Mommy will never forget you!' at the farewell, and Ron noting 'He's lost his marbles.' This arc shows Hagrid's dangerous blind spot for monsters and the tension between his loving nature and poor judgment.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film includes the hatching, Hagrid's delight, the 'he knows his mummy' line, Malfoy at the window, and Hagrid lamenting 'what if the other dragons are mean to him?' The core of the characterisation is present, though some of the more extreme moments (the teddy bear farewell, 'Mommy will never forget you') are compressed or absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film captures the essence of Hagrid's dragon obsession reasonably well. Some of the more extreme, comedic-and-tragic details of his attachment are softened, slightly reducing the portrait of his dangerous naivety, but the core characterisation is substantially preserved.

damaging_scenes.scene: Philosopher's Stone - Hagrid accidentally reveals Fluffy's weakness to the hooded stranger (Film Scene 21)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Harry deduces that the stranger manipulated Hagrid by buying him drinks and exploiting his love of dragons. Hagrid's account is detailed: 'he kept buyin' me drinks... I said, after Fluffy, a dragon would be easy... he had ter be sure I could handle it... So I told him, Fluffy's a piece o' cake if yeh know how to calm him down, jus' play him a bit o' music.' Hagrid's horrified self-realisation ('I shouldn'ta told yeh that!') is a full scene of guilt and dawning horror.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film retains this scene with Hagrid outside shelling peas. Harry asks about the stranger, Hagrid describes being interested in Fluffy and revealing the music trick. The 'I should not have told you that' moment is present. The scene is somewhat compressed but the essential beat is intact.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film handles this scene adequately. Some of the detail about being plied with drinks is present ('a stranger I met down at a pub'). The damage is minimal as the core of Hagrid's vulnerability and the moment of horrified self-realisation are both retained.

damaging_scenes.scene: Philosopher's Stone - Hospital wing: Hagrid's guilt and the photo album gift (Film Scene 21/22)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Hagrid arrives at the hospital wing sobbing with guilt: 'It's -- all -- my -- ruddy -- fault!... I told the evil git how ter get past Fluffy!... Yeh could've died! All fer a dragon egg! I'll never drink again! I should be chucked out an' made ter live as a Muggle!' Harry comforts him and bellows 'VOLDEMORT!' to shock Hagrid out of his crying. Hagrid then gives Harry the photo album, explaining he sent owls to his parents' old school friends. The scene is a full emotional arc of guilt, comfort, and love.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film shows Hagrid arriving at the hospital wing and giving Harry the photo album at the train departure instead. The extended guilt breakdown ('I'll never drink again! I should be chucked out!'), Harry comforting Hagrid, and Harry shouting Voldemort's name to jolt Hagrid out of tears are absent from the hospital scene. The album gift is moved to the platform farewell.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is one of the most emotionally significant Hagrid scenes in the book. His breakdown of guilt, Harry's comforting of him (reversing their usual roles), and Harry's use of Voldemort's name to jolt Hagrid are all character-defining. Moving the album to a brief platform farewell strips the emotional complexity from the scene and loses the role-reversal moment where Harry becomes Hagrid's comforter — a key beat in their relationship's maturation.

damaging_scenes.scene: Philosopher's Stone - Forbidden Forest: Hagrid's characterisation as forest expert and protective guardian (Film Scene 20)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Hagrid leads the forest expedition with authority and expertise: he identifies tracks, evaluates threats ('That wasn' no werewolf an' it wasn' no unicorn'), manages the centaur encounters with familiarity ('Oh, it's you, Ronan... how are yeh?'), expresses impatience with centaur evasiveness ('Never try an' get a straight answer out of a centaur. Ruddy stargazers'), and physically shields Harry and Hermione. He is competent, knowledgeable, and protective throughout.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film retains the key beats of the forest scene but compresses Hagrid's expert commentary. His extended, irritated commentary on the centaurs ('Ruddy stargazers. Not interested in anythin' closer'n the moon') and his detailed forest knowledge are present but abbreviated. The scene is substantially faithful in the corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film's forest scene retains most of Hagrid's competent guardianship. Some of his expert irritability toward centaurs and his fuller knowledge of forest creatures is compressed, but the damage is minor as the essential characterisation is present.

damaging_scenes.scene: Philosopher's Stone - Diagon Alley: Hagrid's explicit comfort and reassurance to Harry at Paddington (not in film)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, over a hamburger at Paddington, Hagrid gives Harry explicit reassurance when Harry voices his fear about not knowing anything and not deserving his fame: 'Don' you worry, Harry. You'll learn fast enough. Everyone starts at the beginning at Hogwarts, you'll be just fine. Just be yerself. I know it's hard. Yeh've been singled out, an' that's always hard. But yeh'll have a great time at Hogwarts -- I did -- still do, 'smatter of fact.' This is the emotional climax of their first day together.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: No equivalent scene exists in the film. The reassurance conversation at Paddington station is absent. Hagrid's emotional attunement to Harry's vulnerability — and his personal identification with Hogwarts as a place of belonging — are never voiced.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This quiet scene is the emotional heart of the Hagrid-Harry first-day bond. Hagrid's personal reassurance ('just be yerself'), his own identification with Hogwarts ('I did -- still do'), and his attunement to Harry's specific fear of inadequacy are all lost. It is the moment that most clearly establishes Hagrid as Harry's first emotional anchor, making the subsequent friendship feel more earned in the book than in the film.

damaging_scenes.scene: Chamber of Secrets - Flourish and Blotts brawl (Film Scene 1, Film Scene 30)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Hagrid physically separates Mr. Weasley and Lucius Malfoy after a brawl has already broken out, then lectures Arthur ('Yeh should've ignored him, Arthur'), nearly lifting him off his feet while straightening his robes, and urges the group to leave. Hagrid is reactive but also takes a moral-advisory role, commenting on the Malfoys' character and shepherding everyone away.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, the physical brawl never happens. Hagrid merely steps forward and puts a firm hand on Mr. Weasley's shoulder before a punch is thrown, stopping the confrontation entirely before it escalates. His subsequent line ('No Malfoy's worth listenin' ter. Rotten ter the core...') is present but the peacekeeper moment is defused rather than reactive.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's version shows Hagrid as physically imposing and pragmatically wise in a messy, reactive situation. The film's pre-emptive intervention is cleaner and less characterful — the book's version of Hagrid wading through chaos and lifting Arthur off the ground is a vivid personality beat that the film loses. Damage is minor since the core sentiment is preserved.

damaging_scenes.scene: Chamber of Secrets - Hagrid's hut, slug-curse visit (Film Scene 2, Film Scene 46)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book visit to Hagrid's cabin after the Mudblood incident is a rich, extended scene: Hagrid makes tea (cementing his jaws with treacle fudge), jokes about signed photos, teases Harry about Ginny, shows off his enormous pumpkins (secretly Engorgement-Charmed), and there is warm, sustained comic banter across the whole visit. The scene establishes Hagrid's humor, his warmth, his subversive wit (telling Lockhart he'd never read one of his books), and his bond with the trio.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film version of the cabin scene is pared down to essentials: Ron vomits slugs into a bucket, Hagrid explains 'Mudblood,' comforts Hermione, and the scene ends. The treacle fudge, the signed-photos joke, the pumpkin patch, the Ginny teasing, and the Lockhart undercutting are all absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book scene is one of the most characterful Hagrid moments in the novel: it shows his sly humor, his self-awareness about Lockhart's fraudulence, his teasing warmth with Harry, and his pride in his (illicit) gardening. The film strips this to a functional expository scene about blood prejudice. Hagrid's wit, humor, and the full texture of his friendship with the trio are significantly reduced.

damaging_scenes.scene: Chamber of Secrets - Hagrid's hut visit under Invisibility Cloak / Azkaban arrest (Film Scene 3, Film Scene 114)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, before Dumbledore and Fudge arrive, Harry and Ron have already begun asking Hagrid about the Chamber. Hagrid is nervous, trembling, and nearly extinguishes the fire — there is a build of tension and pathos. Crucially, Hagrid also delivers his 'follow the spiders' hint, which in the book is spoken while he is aware Harry and Ron are under the cloak and listening. The hint is deliberate and coded.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film preserves the core of this scene well — Hagrid's nervousness, the crossbow, Dumbledore and Fudge arriving, Lucius Malfoy appearing, Hagrid's defiant speech about Dumbledore. The 'follow the spiders' hint is present and dramatically placed. The earlier direct question Harry asks ('Do you know who's opened the Chamber of Secrets?') is added in the film, which actually makes Harry more active. The scene is largely faithful.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film handles this scene reasonably well. The only minor loss is that in the book Hagrid's coded hint feels more emotionally layered — he knows the boys are hidden and is deliberately leaving them a trail. The film version is slightly more mechanical. Damage is minimal.

damaging_scenes.scene: Chamber of Secrets - Harry runs into Hagrid in corridor after diary vision (CUT SCENE — excluded per non-theatrical material note)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, after Harry discovers the truth from the diary, he literally walks into Hagrid in a corridor — Hagrid is carrying a dead rooster, concerned about Harry's appearance, and the encounter reinforces Hagrid's ongoing presence and pastoral concern for Harry even amid the crisis. Harry cannot bring himself to discuss what he's learned, but the encounter humanizes Hagrid at his most vulnerable point in the story.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This scene was cut from the theatrical release. Per the non-theatrical exclusion rule, this material is treated as absent from the film.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The cut removes a moment where Hagrid's warmth and obliviousness to suspicion are shown from Harry's guilty perspective — Harry knowing Hagrid's past while Hagrid remains cheerfully concerned for him is dramatically and emotionally significant. Its loss means the transition from 'Harry learns Hagrid opened the Chamber' to 'Hagrid is arrested' loses a humanizing beat.

damaging_scenes.scene: Chamber of Secrets - Tom Riddle's description of framing Hagrid (Film Scene 3, Scene 133)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Riddle's description of framing Hagrid is more detailed and cutting: 'big, blundering Hagrid, in trouble every other week, trying to raise werewolf cubs under his bed, sneaking off to the Forbidden Forest to wrestle trolls.' Riddle also admits he was surprised the plan worked so well and that he thought someone would see through it — 'as though Hagrid had the brains, or the power!' This makes Hagrid's innocence and the injustice of his framing more pointed, and implicitly dignifies Hagrid by noting Riddle underestimated the credulity of the system.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's Riddle simply says 'It was my word against Hagrid's. Only Dumbledore seemed to think Hagrid was innocent.' The extended characterization of Hagrid as an easy mark — and Riddle's own arrogance about pulling it off — is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's version adds dimension to both the injustice done to Hagrid and to Riddle's calculated cruelty. The film's truncation means the audience gets less sense of how Hagrid was specifically victimized and what Riddle thought of him. Minor damage since the core framing revelation is intact.

damaging_scenes.scene: Chamber of Secrets - End feast, Hagrid's return (Film Scene 3, Scene 137)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Hagrid returns to the end-of-year feast and 'cuffing Harry and Ron so hard on the shoulders that they were knocked into their plates of trifle.' It is a physical, exuberant, unselfconscious expression of affection — very characteristic of Hagrid.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, Hagrid enters the Great Hall nervously, looks around embarrassed, thanks Harry, Ron and Hermione verbally, and Harry replies 'There's no Hogwarts without you, Hagrid.' Dumbledore then leads a standing ovation. The physical cuffing is absent; the emotional register is more sentimental and restrained.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's version of Hagrid's return is physically boisterous — he knocks the boys into their food, which is deeply in character. The film replaces this with a more staged, emotionally earnest tableau. The line 'There's no Hogwarts without you, Hagrid' is a film addition that, while warm, tips the scene into sentiment rather than the book's rougher, funnier affection. Minor damage to voice and texture.

damaging_scenes.scene: Chamber of Secrets - Quidditch match commentary (Film Scene 2, Scene 65)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book does not position Hagrid as a Quidditch commentator in this scene — he is a spectator.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film gives Hagrid brief commentary lines during the Quidditch match ('Gallopin' Gorgons! Slytherin's flyin' like they got dragon fire in their brooms...'; 'Blimey, Harry's got 'imself a Rogue Bludger!'). These are film-original lines that add color.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is actually a net-neutral or slight positive for characterization — the film-original commentary is consistent with Hagrid's voice and enthusiasm. It is not an unfaithful moment that causes damage. Including for completeness but scoring as minimal.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 6 (Paddock/Hippogriff lesson) — Hagrid's aside to Harry after the ride
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 42: Harry tells Malfoy to shut up because 'Hagrid was looking downcast and Harry wanted Hagrid's first lesson to be a success.' Hagrid loses his thread after Malfoy's mockery but retains a sense of wounded dignity; the class dynamic shows him genuinely rattled but still managing. Book Scene 40: Hagrid says uncertainly 'I -- I thought they were funny,' showing vulnerability but also genuine puzzlement rather than seeking Harry's validation.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 6: After Harry's successful ride, Hagrid leans in and whispers 'How'm I doin' me firs' day?' to Harry, directly soliciting reassurance from a student mid-lesson. Harry replies 'Brilliant... Professor.' This repositions Harry as Hagrid's emotional anchor and supervisor rather than a supportive friend.
damaging_scenes.explanation: In the books, Hagrid's insecurity about his first lesson is conveyed through narration and his rattled responses to Malfoy — it is internalized and observed by Harry with sympathy. Having Hagrid directly ask a thirteen-year-old student 'How'm I doing?' mid-lesson undercuts his authority more sharply than the books intend and makes the dependency on Harry explicit in a way that diminishes Hagrid's stature as a teacher rather than showing his relatable vulnerability.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 6 (Paddock) — Hagrid brings only one hippogriff vs. the full herd
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 47–74: Hagrid arrives with a dozen hippogriffs on chains, conducts the full class through bowing exercises with multiple beasts, has students including Ron and Hermione practice on the chestnut hippogriff, and Neville struggles with his own animal. The lesson is a genuine, ambitious pedagogical event — chaotic but substantive.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 6: Only Buckbeak is present. The lesson collapses to a single interaction between Harry and one creature, with no classroom management of multiple animals, no other students practicing bowing, and no sense of Hagrid orchestrating a whole lesson.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Reducing the lesson to one hippogriff strips Hagrid of the demonstration of his genuine, if over-ambitious, teaching competence. The books show he has a real plan — bring a herd, teach the protocol, let the whole class engage. The film version makes the lesson feel accidental and thin, reinforcing the 'oaf' reading Malfoy voices rather than the complex picture of an enthusiast who simply misjudges the level.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 6 (Paddock) — Hagrid lifts Harry onto Buckbeak without instruction
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 66–70: Hagrid gives Harry clear, calm instructions on how to mount — 'Yeh climb up there, jus' behind the wing joint... mind yeh don' pull any of his feathers out.' Harry then mounts by his own effort, putting his foot on the wing and hoisting himself. Hagrid slaps the hindquarters only after Harry is seated.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 6: Hagrid physically lifts Harry high and drops him onto Buckbeak's back, then slaps the hindquarters before Harry has settled — the script note reads 'before Harry's settled.' Harry slides scarily back as the wings unfold.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book Hagrid is attentive to safety protocols within his own eccentric framework — he gives careful mounting instructions. The film version has him manhandle Harry onto the animal before he is ready, which plays as comic buffoonery and reinforces the 'dangerous oaf' framing at the expense of Hagrid's genuine, if unorthodox, care for his students. It also removes Harry's small act of self-directed courage in mounting the beast himself.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 6 (Paddock) — Hagrid's response after Malfoy is slashed
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 79: Hagrid immediately takes charge — 'Yer not dyin'! ... Someone help me -- gotta get him outta here.' He is shaken ('gone very white') but functional. He calls for help, has Hermione hold the gate, lifts Malfoy, and runs with him to the castle — decisive crisis management despite his distress.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 6: Hagrid shouts 'Calm yerself! Yer fine... jus' a scratch,' then looks at the gash, says 'No. I'm the teacher. You all... you all just... Class dismissed!' and 'swoops up Malfoy, flops him over his shoulder, and lumbers toward the castle.' The dismissal line 'You all just...' trails off incoherently before he recovers.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The trailing, incoherent 'You all just...' and the belated assertion 'I'm the teacher' reads as Hagrid losing composure and reasserting authority unconvincingly, whereas the book version shows him immediately functional under pressure. Minor, but it nudges Hagrid toward incompetence rather than rattled competence.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 13 (Hagrid's hut, pre-execution) — Hagrid engineers Ron/Hermione reconciliation
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book's pre-execution hut visit (Book Scenes 278–310) focuses entirely on Hagrid's barely-contained grief and the trio's attempts to comfort him. Hagrid does not stage-manage the friends' quarrel; he is too consumed by the approaching execution. The Ron/Hermione conflict appears in the book corpus (e.g., Scene 235–236) but Hagrid's role there is to gently chide them about Hermione, not to orchestrate hugging rituals.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 13: In the final hut visit before the execution, Hagrid — on the verge of watching his beloved animal be killed — pauses to direct Harry and Ron to shake hands and then orders Hermione and Ron to hug, coaching them through 'the most awkward hug Hogwarts has ever seen' and commenting 'Crikey, tha's jus' abou' the most pathetic hug I e'er seen.' This comic interlude occupies significant screen time in what should be a scene of devastating emotional weight.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's pre-execution scene is one of the most emotionally raw Hagrid moments in the series — 'helplessness worse to watch than tears.' Converting it into a comedy beat where Hagrid plays relationship counsellor badly damages the tonal integrity of his arc and of the scene. It also reframes Hagrid's emotional state: instead of a man barely holding himself together, he is a cheerful mediator. This is the most damaging single scene in the corpus because it actively replaces faithful characterisation with a contradictory one at a climactic emotional moment.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 9 & 10 (Black Lake) — Buckbeak's verdict delivered outdoors, Hagrid skimming stones
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 167–209: Hagrid receives the verdict letter while alone in his hut, and the trio finds him collapsed, sobbing uncontrollably, 'his face glazed with tears.' The scene is private, interior, and devastated. Hagrid's grief is unguarded and overwhelming.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scenes 9–10: Hagrid is outside at the Black Lake in his court suit, skimming giant rocks and delivering the verdict news conversationally in the open. His eyes are 'red with tears' but he is functional and composed enough to skim rocks and recount the hearing. He delivers 'Buckbeak's bin sentenced ter death' as a revelation to the trio rather than receiving comfort from them in a state of collapse.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book scene of Hagrid's post-verdict collapse — including his confession about Azkaban, his terror of returning, and his helpless love for Buckbeak — is largely displaced. The film replaces raw private grief with a composed outdoor scene. While some emotional content survives, the depth of Hagrid's vulnerability, his Azkaban trauma, and his moral fear of breaking the law are absent from this corpus, reducing the scene's emotional and character weight considerably.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 8 (Three Broomsticks back room) — Hagrid's role in the Sirius/Potters backstory
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 138–149: Hagrid is a major voice in the Three Broomsticks conversation. He interjects emotionally ('Filthy, stinkin' turncoat!'), tells the central story of rescuing baby Harry, describes Sirius giving him the motorbike, and delivers the chilling line about what he would have done to Black: 'I'd 've ripped him limb -- from -- limb.' He is a primary narrator and an emotionally grounded witness to the Potters' deaths.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 8: Hagrid is physically present (he rips the door off the Three Broomsticks) but the corpus contains no lines from him inside the back room conversation. The scene cuts inside only to Harry's POV through the window, and the dialogue shown is between Fudge, McGonagall, and Rosmerta. Hagrid's testimony about rescuing Harry, his grief, his rage at Black, and his personal connection to the Potters' story are not evidenced in the film corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses this scene to establish Hagrid as a living witness to the worst night of Harry's family history, deepening both their relationship and his emotional stakes in the Sirius Black plot. If the film corpus is representative and Hagrid does not deliver his testimony in this scene, a significant piece of his characterisation as someone personally wounded by the Potters' deaths — and therefore someone Harry can understand more fully — is lost.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 12 (Sundial Garden / pre-execution visit) — 'I say we set him free' line given to Harry
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 208: It is Hagrid himself who voices the thought of letting Buckbeak go — 'Thought o' jus' letting Buckbeak go... tryin' ter make him fly away' — but explains why he cannot: the legal consequences and his fear of Azkaban. This is a moment of genuine moral conflict and self-revelation from Hagrid.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 12: Harry says 'I say we set him free.' Hagrid responds by explaining why he cannot — the Dumbledore complication. The originating moral impulse transfers entirely to Harry.
damaging_scenes.explanation: In the book, Hagrid's own articulation of this thought — and his agonised rejection of it — is a key character moment showing his internal conflict between love for the animal and terror of lawbreaking. Moving the line to Harry makes Hagrid passive (reactive rather than conflicted) and gives Harry credit for moral initiative that the book assigns to Hagrid's own wrestling conscience.

damaging_scenes.scene: Goblet of Fire - Hagrid's dragon reveal scene (midnight walk with Harry and Madame Maxime)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Hagrid secretively arranges a midnight meeting with Harry, leads him under the Invisibility Cloak to witness the dragons, and the scene is thick with Hagrid's characteristic wonder and reverence for dangerous creatures ('Is'n' it beautiful?'). Hagrid is also clearly aware Harry is there the whole time — he arranged the meeting for Harry's benefit, whispering to him to keep quiet and stay covered. The scene is about Hagrid's loyalty and protectiveness toward Harry, giving him a crucial advantage at personal risk.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, Hagrid leads Harry out with a big red flower, having combed his hair, and the framing emphasises the romantic date with Madame Maxime far more than any protective gesture toward Harry. Hagrid's line 'These are seriously misunderstood creatures' and his excited commentary ('that Horntail is a right nasty piece of work') is present, but the film strips the scene of its book context: there is no whispered instruction, no sense that Hagrid has orchestrated this specifically to help Harry survive. The romantic subplot dominates the scene's tone.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book scene is a clear act of deliberate, calculated loyalty — Hagrid risks trouble to give Harry a fighting chance. The film collapses this into a romantic excursion that Harry happens to witness. Hagrid's protective agency toward Harry is muted, reducing the emotional weight of a defining friendship moment.

damaging_scenes.scene: Goblet of Fire - Yule Ball: Hagrid dancing with Madame Maxime, hand slipping to her backside
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book presents Hagrid and Madame Maxime waltzing through the students at the Yule Ball, cutting a wide path, with Hagrid clearly smitten. The portrayal is warm and dignified in its own way — a large, awkward man genuinely enchanted. The romance is played tenderly, consistent with how the books describe Hagrid's 'rapt, misty-eyed expression' when near her.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film adds a sight gag where Hagrid's hand slips down to Madame Maxime's buttocks during the dance, and she has to push it back up. This is played for comedy.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Hagrid is socially naive and earnest, not crudely lecherous. The gag cheapens his romantic sincerity and plays his size and awkwardness for low comedy in a moment the book treats with genuine warmth. It slightly coarsens a character whose tenderness is one of his defining traits.

damaging_scenes.scene: Goblet of Fire - After Second Task: Hagrid's toast at the hut ('Soon to be the youngest Triwizard champion there's ever been!')
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book corpus does not contain a post-second-task hut celebration scene with a toast. In the book, Hagrid's supportive role around the second task is expressed through his unicorn lesson check-in ('Yeh're goin' ter be fine... I'd've bin worried before I saw yeh take on tha Horntail') and his general encouragement. His relationship with Harry is built across many small, private moments of faith and warmth.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film creates a scene at Hagrid's hut with Ron, Hermione, and Harry where Hagrid gives a speech and toasts Harry as 'soon to be the youngest Triwizard champion there's ever been.' While warm in intent, this is a film invention that condenses Hagrid's support into a single public-facing moment.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor in isolation, but the film's Hagrid tends to express his affection for Harry in broad, celebratory gestures rather than the quieter, private moments of the book (the unicorn lesson reassurance, the post-Skeeter recovery scene, etc.). This reflects a broader flattening of the relationship's texture, though this individual scene is not significantly harmful.

damaging_scenes.scene: Goblet of Fire - Hagrid's half-giant revelation and emotional withdrawal are entirely absent from the film
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book dedicates substantial space to the Rita Skeeter article outing Hagrid as half-giant, his subsequent withdrawal and emotional collapse, the trio's repeated attempts to reach him, Dumbledore's intervention, and Hagrid's tearful recovery — culminating in him showing Harry a photograph of his father and making a speech about never being ashamed of what you are. This arc defines Hagrid's vulnerability, his insecurity about prejudice, his history, and his relationship with Dumbledore. It also deepens Harry's loyalty and demonstrates Hermione's fierce protectiveness.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film contains none of this arc. There is no Rita Skeeter article about Hagrid's parentage, no withdrawal, no Dumbledore visit to the cabin, no photograph of his father, no 'never be ashamed' speech. The only reference to Hagrid's background is a brief, tonally light conversation during the midnight dragon walk where Hagrid mentions his mother left when he was three and his father died when he started school — delivered as romantic small talk to Madame Maxime rather than as a moment of vulnerability.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the largest single damage to Hagrid's adaptation. An entire emotional and thematic arc — prejudice, shame, identity, resilience, the Dumbledore relationship, and the depth of the trio's loyalty — is completely absent. The film's Hagrid has no inner life beyond warmth and enthusiasm. The book's Hagrid is a character who wrestles with stigma and finds courage; the film's Hagrid is a background presence. The 'never be ashamed' speech is one of the book's most thematically resonant Hagrid moments and it is entirely lost.

damaging_scenes.scene: Goblet of Fire - Hagrid confronting Karkaroff after Krum is attacked in the forest
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, when Karkaroff spits at Dumbledore's feet and makes accusations, Hagrid physically seizes Karkaroff, lifts him off the ground, slams him against a tree, and demands he apologise — showing fierce, instinctive loyalty to Dumbledore. Dumbledore has to firmly order him to stop. Hagrid then escorts Harry back to the castle, ranting about Karkaroff's disrespect for Dumbledore and lecturing Harry about trusting foreign students, before calming down.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This scene does not appear in the film corpus. The forest scene with Krum being attacked and Karkaroff's confrontation with Dumbledore is absent from the provided film material.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book scene showcases Hagrid's fierce protectiveness of Dumbledore, his capacity for genuine intimidation when provoked, and a more complex side of his personality — loyal to a fault, briefly hot-headed, then self-correcting. The film loses a moment where Hagrid acts with real force and consequence. His relationship with Dumbledore as something he would physically defend is never demonstrated in the film.

damaging_scenes.scene: Goblet of Fire - Post-Voldemort-return scene: Hagrid's wisdom and steadiness ('What's comin' will come, an' we'll meet it when it does')
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book ends with a significant scene in Hagrid's cabin where Hagrid offers Harry, Ron, and Hermione grounded, courageous wisdom about Voldemort's return: 'Knew he was goin' ter come back... we'll fight... What's comin' will come, an' we'll meet it when it does.' He also tells Harry 'Yeh did as much as yer father would've done' — one of the most emotionally resonant lines in the book for Harry. Hagrid is shown as a figure of moral steadiness and comfort at the saga's darkest turning point. Dumbledore has also summoned him for a secret mission.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This cabin scene does not appear in the film corpus. The film ends with Harry returning to the Dursleys without this scene.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The loss of this closing scene removes Hagrid's most important moment of the entire book at its thematic climax. His comparison of Harry to his father, his calm courage in the face of Voldemort's return, and his role as an anchor of warmth and resilience at the saga's darkest hour are all absent. The film's Hagrid never functions as a source of moral wisdom or emotional grounding — only as a friendly background figure. This significantly diminishes his role in the wider saga.

damaging_scenes.scene: Goblet of Fire - Blast-Ended Skrewts arc: extended Care of Magical Creatures teaching entirely absent from film
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book devotes considerable space to Hagrid's Care of Magical Creatures lessons: the skrewts, his enthusiasm, his defensiveness under Malfoy's mockery, his sharp put-down of Malfoy ('I hear yeh made a good ferret'), his determination after the Rita Skeeter article, the unicorn lessons, the niffler lesson, and his general characterisation as an eccentric but genuinely knowledgeable and passionate teacher who loves his subject even when his choices are questionable.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film contains no Care of Magical Creatures lessons at all. Hagrid is entirely absent from the classroom context in the film corpus. His identity as a teacher — one of his two main roles in the book and a source of much characterisation — is completely unrepresented.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Hagrid-as-teacher is a crucial dimension of his Book 4 characterisation: his passion, his blind spots, his vulnerability to criticism, his resilience, and his moments of genuine competence (unicorns, nifflers) are all expressed through these scenes. Stripping them entirely reduces him to gamekeeper-and-friend, erasing a whole register of his personality and the professional pride that makes the Skeeter attack so devastating.

damaging_scenes.scene: Goblet of Fire - Hagrid's mocking of Moody ('Moody gave it to me. That day we had tea') and friendship with Moody implied in the book
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book shows Hagrid and Moody drinking together at the Three Broomsticks, with Hagrid appearing to be on genuinely friendly terms with Moody — Moody taps Hagrid to alert him to Harry's invisible presence, and Hagrid arranges the midnight dragon visit having apparently been 'nudged' by Moody (as revealed by fake-Moody at the end). This friendship is a meaningful piece of dramatic irony: Hagrid trusts someone who is manipulating him.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film corpus, after the third task when fake-Moody is revealed, 'Moody' is shown mocking Hagrid's voice ('These are seriously misunderstood creatures') in a dismissive, contemptuous way. The film uses this to signal Crouch Jr.'s contempt, but it inadvertently frames the dragon-reveal scene retrospectively as pure manipulation with no warmth — erasing the dramatic irony of Hagrid being genuinely deceived by someone he trusted.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor but worth noting: the film's mocking impersonation slightly cheapens what in the book is a poignant irony — Hagrid's trusting nature being exploited. The audience is directed to laugh at Hagrid rather than feel the sting of his betrayal.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 – Hagrid returns to his hut; Umbridge interrogation and story of giants
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes an extended, richly detailed scene ('Hagrid's Tale') in which Hagrid recounts his full mission to the giants: the month-long covert journey, the diplomatic gifts of Gubraithian fire and goblin-made helmet, the Gurg Karkus, the overnight violence that killed Karkus and replaced him with the hostile Golgomath, Hagrid and Olympe's courageous persistence over weeks, their nightly cave visits to wounded giants, the Death Eater presence of Macnair, and ultimately a partial but meaningful contact with dissident giants. This is a long, carefully staged scene with Hagrid as the sole narrator of a genuinely important diplomatic mission, demonstrating his bravery, loyalty to Dumbledore, strategic patience, and emotional complexity.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film collapses the entire account into a few lines: 'Dumbledore sent me to parlay with the giants… I tried to convince them to join the cause. But I wasn't the only one trying to win them over… Death Eaters.' Then Hagrid says 'I gave them Dumbledore's message. Suppose some of them remember he was friendly to them, I suppose' – a line bizarrely delivered in the third person as if quoting Dumbledore. All the diplomatic detail, the weeks of effort, the Macnair identification, the cave visits, the Gurg succession, and Olympe's role are excised entirely.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's 'Hagrid's Tale' chapter is the primary vehicle for establishing Hagrid as a brave, active agent in the war against Voldemort rather than merely a gentle giant gamekeeper. It shows him carrying out a dangerous covert mission with skill, persistence and emotional intelligence over an extended period. The film reduces this to a two-sentence summary, stripping Hagrid of his war-role agency entirely and giving the audience no sense of what he risked or achieved. This also removes crucial world-building about giant society that pays off later in the saga.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 – Hagrid returns to hut; physical injuries and emotional state
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book devotes significant space to the horror of Hagrid's injuries on his return: matted blood, a puffy eye, many cuts and broken ribs, obvious fresh trauma. His stoic deflection ('It's nuthin'') combined with visible distress gives him a complex heroic-wounded quality. His repeated insistence on minimising his injuries while placing a dragon steak on his eye is both comic and deeply touching – a characterisation beat that is entirely his own.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film shows Hagrid injured and uses the dragon steak briefly, but the emotional weight of Hagrid's stoic deflection and the sustained comedic-tender interplay around the steak (dropping it, Fang eating it, slapping it back) is almost entirely absent. The injuries are noted but not dwelt upon with any affective texture.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The dragon steak business in the book is a defining character-voice moment – warmly comic, self-deprecating, proud – that communicates Hagrid's personality more economically than dialogue. Its reduction flattens his return scene and reduces audience investment in his suffering.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 – Grawp introduction in the Forbidden Forest
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book presents the Grawp reveal as a multi-stage, slowly escalating dread sequence: the long trek into the Forest, Hagrid's nervous pre-explanation, Hermione's horrified reaction, the explicit detail of Grawp's misshapen proportions, Hagrid's tearful admission of brotherhood, the dangerous near-miss when Grawp grabs for Hermione, Hagrid being knocked down by his own brother, and Harry and Hermione's genuine terror combined with reluctant pity. Hagrid is shown as simultaneously deluded, loving, reckless and pitiful – a carefully balanced emotional portrait.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film presents the Grawp scene in an abbreviated and somewhat lighter register. Hermione is picked up by Grawp but then put down and talks firmly to him ('Put me down! Now!'), which Grawp obeys, and Ron hits Grawp's leg with a stick. The scene is played more as comedic spectacle. Hagrid's tearful breakdown ('I couldn't just leave him, because, because he's my brother') is present but undercut by the lighter tone of the surrounding beats.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Grawp scene carefully balances horror with pathos to produce a morally complex portrait of Hagrid's love as simultaneously beautiful and dangerous. The film tips it toward comedy, losing the genuine dread and the full weight of Hagrid's delusion and grief, which diminishes the emotional complexity of his characterisation at a key moment.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 – Hagrid's Thestral lesson under Umbridge inspection
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book gives a detailed account of Umbridge's inspection of Hagrid's Thestral lesson. She uses conspicuously slow, loud speech and mime as though Hagrid cannot understand normal English – a calculated act of humiliation targeting his giant heritage. Hermione shakes with fury, Pansy laughs that Hagrid sounds 'like grunting'. Hagrid's face flushes but he 'ploughs on valiantly'. The book makes explicit that this is bigotry directed at his half-giant status and shows Hagrid maintaining dignity under extraordinary provocation.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus does not contain this Thestral lesson inspection scene. Umbridge is present in the film and does visit Hagrid's hut, but the systematic public humiliation of Hagrid's lesson – the mime, the slow loud speech, the 'grunting' comment, Hagrid's flushed but dignified response – does not appear in the provided film corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The inspection scene is the clearest dramatisation of the anti-half-breed prejudice Hagrid faces and shows his most dignified characterisation: continuing to teach under humiliation without breaking. Its absence removes the thematic argument that Umbridge's campaign against Hagrid is rooted in racism, and strips Hagrid of a moment that reveals his quiet courage as a professional.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 – Hogsmeade pub scene; Hagrid alone and mournful
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book includes a scene at the Three Broomsticks where Harry finds Hagrid sitting alone, clearly miserable, with fresh injuries he refuses to explain. Hagrid articulates a philosophy of kinship and orphanhood ('Both outsiders… both orphans'), reflects on the importance of family, and shows a deeper melancholy rooted in his own fractured history. He is emotionally raw, philosophically reflective, and withdrawing from Harry in a way that signals serious psychological strain.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This scene does not appear in the provided film corpus. There is no equivalent of Hagrid alone at the pub, the orphan-bonding conversation, or his mournful philosophical reflection on blood and family.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The pub scene is one of the few moments in book five where Hagrid's emotional interior is directly expressed and where his relationship with Harry is developed on a basis of shared outsider identity. Its absence removes depth from their bond and removes a layer of Hagrid's characterisation as a lonely, complex figure rather than simply a cheerful gentle giant.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 – Hagrid's attempted sacking (Astronomy Tower battle)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book depicts Hagrid resisting arrest with extraordinary physical power (Stunners bouncing off him due to giant blood), throwing an attacker ten feet, and carrying Fang on his shoulders while roaring 'COWARDS! RUDDY COWARDS!' before fleeing to join Dumbledore. It is a scene of fierce, almost primal dignity. The book also provides aftermath discussion: Ron and Hermione confirming his giant blood explains the Stunner resistance, and Hermione's tearful distress at losing both Dumbledore and Hagrid.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus does not contain this scene. The battle outside Hagrid's cabin, Hagrid resisting multiple Stunners, throwing an attacker, roaring his defiance and fleeing with Fang – none of this appears in the provided film corpus text.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is Hagrid's most heroic moment in the entire book – a physical manifestation of his refusal to be defeated quietly and a direct parallel to Dumbledore's own escape from Fudge's men. Its absence from the film corpus means Hagrid loses his most powerful display of courage and defiant agency, and the emotional cost of his departure is not dramatised for the audience.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 – Hagrid leads trio to Grawp during Quidditch match (motivation and framing)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes that Hagrid brings Harry and Hermione to see Grawp during the Quidditch match because he fears imminent sacking and needs to secure caretakers for his brother before he goes. He is emotionally overwhelmed, crying openly, and the scene is framed as a desperate act of love from a man who knows he is running out of time. He explicitly tells them he would leave immediately to avoid public humiliation 'like Trelawney' but cannot go without securing Grawp's future.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film presents Hagrid approaching Harry during the Quidditch match and leading them to Grawp, with Hagrid saying 'I'll likely be getting the sack any day now… I just couldn't leave without telling someone about him.' The basic motivation is preserved but the emotional texture – Hagrid's tears, his specific fear of public humiliation, his reference to Trelawney – is greatly compressed.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film retains the functional story beat but loses the emotional granularity that makes Hagrid's decision sympathetic rather than merely reckless. Minor damage given the core motivation is communicated.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 – Post-return; Hagrid warns 'there's a storm coming'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book does not give Hagrid a prophetic 'storm coming' speech. His warning function is delivered through his account of the giants' situation and the presence of Death Eaters, not through a standalone atmospheric pronouncement.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film gives Hagrid the line 'It's changing out there. Just like last time. There's a storm coming, Harry. We'd all best be ready when she does.' This is a Hollywood-style portentous speech not present in the book corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: While minor, this line replaces Hagrid's authentic voice (earthy, specific, grounded in concrete events) with a generic dramatic-warning register that belongs to a different character archetype. It slightly misrepresents how Hagrid communicates threat and gravity.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Hagrid rescues Katie Bell on the road outside Hogsmeade
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Harry runs for help, collides with Hagrid on the lane, explains what happened, and Hagrid takes charge by scooping Katie up and running to the castle. It is a reactive, practical rescue — Hagrid acts swiftly but without any special calming magic or tenderness beyond his physical capability.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has Hagrid emerge dramatically from the white, press his face close to Katie's and whisper 'Now, now. Now, now...' as a soothing mantra until her body goes limp — a quasi-magical, almost shamanistic calming act not present in the books. The film also collapses the geography: Harry does not run for help and collide with Hagrid separately; Hagrid just appears.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film invents a mystical tenderness to Hagrid's rescue that flatters him beyond what the books establish. More importantly, it removes the beat where Harry runs for help and physically bumps into Hagrid — a small but character-consistent moment of Hagrid being encountered in his natural habitat going about his business. The invented 'whispering calm' replaces practical giant strength with a softer, almost magical quality the books never give him, subtly shifting his characterisation.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Hagrid at Aragog's burial / outdoor scene
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book stages an elaborate, emotionally rich evening: Harry arrives under the Invisibility Cloak, Hagrid is overcome with grief and has made himself a black armband, he has already dug the grave, they discuss Aragog's history and the danger from the colony, Slughorn sneaks venom from the pincers while Hagrid isn't looking, Hagrid gives a eulogising speech, they carry him inside, drink toasts over hours, Hagrid and Slughorn sing, Hagrid becomes tearful about Harry's parents, and the whole thing functions as the mechanism by which Felix Felicis manoeuvres Harry into getting the memory. The burial itself is full of tragicomic bathos — Hagrid rolling the giant corpse into the pit with a 'horrible crunchy thud,' Slughorn pocketing venom, etc.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film condenses the outdoor burial significantly. Hagrid sits on a stump when Harry and Slughorn arrive. There is no black armband, no account of retrieving Aragog's body from the colony, no mention that the colony now won't let Hagrid approach, no long excavation of their shared history. Slughorn speaks his eulogy, Hagrid tips Aragog into the grave, and they move inside. The rich tragicomic texture and Hagrid's layered grief backstory are compressed into a brief, functional scene.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The compression removes the most distinctively Hagrid-ish quality of the sequence: his completely incongruous, total-commitment grief for a creature that tried to eat his friends, combined with the darkly funny detail that even the colony won't let him near now Aragog is gone. This is prime Hagrid characterisation — his love for dangerous creatures taken to its absurd, sincere extreme. The film retains the emotional shell but strips the substance that makes Hagrid's grief both funny and genuinely touching.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Interior of Hagrid's hut, drinking scene
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book gives Hagrid substantial interior life and dialogue during the drinking scene: he presses the unicorn tail on Slughorn, he makes extravagant toasts, he becomes tearful about Harry's parents ('Me dad was no age ter go... nor were yer mum an' dad, Harry'), grasps Harry's arm, and his snoring in the background is the backdrop against which Harry finally persuades Slughorn to give up the memory. Hagrid functions as an emotional anchor and unwitting co-conspirator in the Felix Felicis plan.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has Hagrid fall asleep almost immediately after the 'poof' exchange about his fish. He snores through the rest of the scene. His emotional contribution — the toasts, the tears about Harry's parents, the arm-grasping, the unicorn tail gift — is either eliminated or drastically reduced. The scene pivots almost entirely to Slughorn and Harry once Hagrid goes under.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Hagrid's emotional warmth and his sorrow about Harry's parents is a key humanising beat in this scene. Having him simply pass out early converts him from an active emotional presence into a piece of furniture — a warm body whose snoring provides atmosphere for the Harry/Slughorn confrontation. His grief for Harry's parents and his spontaneous generosity (the unicorn tail) are lost, reducing his function in the scene to near zero.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Hagrid after Dumbledore's death / outside the hut
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Hagrid has been fighting the Death Eaters outside his cabin and his house is set on fire. He emerges carrying Fang on his back. He and Harry have an extended, painful exchange where Harry tries to tell Hagrid that Dumbledore is dead, Hagrid refuses to believe it (thinking Snape must have been maintaining his cover on Dumbledore's orders), and Harry chooses not to argue. Hagrid then puts his hands under Harry's arms and lifts him upright. They put out the fire together using Aguamenti, Hagrid raising his pink umbrella. Hagrid says 'Nothin Dumbledore won't be able to put right.' Then as they approach the castle, Hagrid gradually works out from the crowd what has happened.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has Hagrid stumble out of the burning hut and immediately say 'if anybody can put it right, Dumbledore can' — but critically, the extended exchange where Harry tries and fails to tell Hagrid the truth, and where Hagrid's loyalty and denial are movingly dramatised, is compressed. The film Hagrid simply asks 'Where's Dumbledore?' and goes still when Harry cannot speak. The joint Aguamenti fire-fighting is absent. The detail of Hagrid carrying Fang on his back is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's version of this scene is one of Hagrid's finest moments: his absolute refusal to believe Dumbledore could be dead, and his loyal rationalisation that Snape must be acting under orders, reveal the depth of his faith in Dumbledore and his fundamental decency. The film collapses this to a single stunned silence. The practical detail of them fighting the fire together — Hagrid with his pink umbrella — is also lost, a characteristically Hagrid-ish beat that mixes the comic and the poignant.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Chase scene: Hagrid fighting Death Eaters
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book shows Hagrid emerging from his cabin and actively trying to stop the Death Eaters escaping — firing curses, being hit by curse after curse from the blond Death Eater, his toughened giant-inherited skin protecting him. Harry's internal voice says 'not Hagrid... not Hagrid too.' The fight is extended: the Death Eater shouts 'Incendio' and Hagrid's house explodes in flames, Hagrid bellows about Fang being inside. Harry can hear Hagrid yelling and Fang howling throughout his own duel with Snape.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film corpus (Scene 9), Hagrid's active fighting role is reduced. The fire is set by Bellatrix, and Hagrid stumbles out afterwards. The extended parallel action of Hagrid duelling the blond Death Eater while Harry duels Snape — establishing Hagrid's courage and physical resilience — is not present in the film corpus as a dramatised sequence. Hagrid's yelling about Fang ('Fang's in there, yer evil—!') and the ongoing battle cries are absent from the film version.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses this scene to show Hagrid's bravery directly — he comes out fighting, absorbs curses, and his sheer physical toughness is shown under fire. Harry's fear for him ('not Hagrid too') establishes the emotional stakes. The film reduces Hagrid to a victim of the fire rather than an active combatant, diminishing his agency in one of the saga's climactic action sequences and weakening the emotional resonance of Harry's protective instinct toward him.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Hagrid carries Dumbledore's body to the funeral / attends McGonagall's meeting
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book has Hagrid carry Dumbledore's body wrapped in purple velvet spangled with gold to the funeral, walking slowly up the aisle crying silently. He attends the senior staff meeting in McGonagall's office, where he is asked for his views on whether Hogwarts should remain open, and gives a deeply moving answer: 'It's me home, it's bin me home since I was thirteen.' He also growls 'No other headmaster or headmistress ever gave more to this school' — a fierce tribute. He sits at the funeral next to Grawp, who pats him hard on the head.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus contains no scene of Hagrid carrying Dumbledore's body to the funeral, no staff meeting in McGonagall's office, and no equivalent of Hagrid's speech about Hogwarts being his home. The funeral cortege and Hagrid's role in it are absent from the provided film corpus. Hagrid appears in the crowd scene outside the castle (Scene 10) but his named role in the funeral itself is not present.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Hagrid carrying Dumbledore to burial is one of the most important symbolic acts assigned to him in the series — it literalises his role as Dumbledore's most loyal servant and reflects back to the very opening of Philosopher's Stone where Hagrid carried baby Harry. The loss of the staff meeting removes Hagrid's most articulate and emotionally weighted speech of the entire book. 'It's been me home since I was thirteen' and his fierce defence of Dumbledore's legacy are defining character moments; their absence is a significant arc-level loss.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Hagrid's sulking / reconciliation scene at his cabin
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book devotes a substantial scene to Hagrid's hurt at being dropped by his three favourite students, his passive-aggressive sulking (failing to notice them in corridors), Harry's forceful knocking and threat to blast the door in, Hagrid's wounded dignity ('I'm a teacher! A teacher, Potter!'), and the sharp, affectionate exchange ('Since when have you called me sir?' / 'Since when have you called me Potter?'). The scene establishes Hagrid's emotional complexity — pride, hurt, loyalty — and the genuine friendship dynamic.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This scene does not appear in the film corpus. There is no equivalent of the reconciliation scene, Hagrid's sulking period, or the 'I'm a teacher, Potter' confrontation.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is one of the richest relationship scenes between Harry and Hagrid in the entire book. The fact that Hagrid has enough wounded pride to shut them out, and that Harry has to force his way back in using Hagrid's own logic against him, shows both characters at their most three-dimensional. Its total absence from the film means the audience loses the texture of this friendship — particularly Hagrid's dignity and capacity for genuine hurt — and the Aragog burial scene that follows loses its emotional setup.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Hagrid overhears Snape/Dumbledore argument and tells Harry
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book has a significant late-night corridor scene where Hagrid, having come from the hospital wing after Ron's poisoning, inadvertently reveals to Harry and Hermione that he overheard a heated argument between Dumbledore and Snape in which Snape said he didn't want to 'do it anymore' and Dumbledore told him he'd agreed and that was that. This is a crucial piece of dramatic irony — the audience and Harry misread it as Snape resisting his spy role, when it actually foreshadows Snape's agreement to kill Dumbledore if necessary. Hagrid also defends Hogwarts staying open and worries about a repeat of Chamber of Secrets.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This scene does not appear in the film corpus. There is no equivalent of Hagrid inadvertently dropping this information about Snape and Dumbledore's argument.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This scene is important for two reasons: it uses Hagrid as an unwitting conduit for one of the book's central pieces of dramatic irony (Snape's reluctance to kill Dumbledore, misread as disloyalty), and it shows Hagrid's insider knowledge of Hogwarts while demonstrating his characteristic inability to keep a secret. Both functions — the narrative irony and the character beat — are lost. The film also loses Hagrid's broader anxiety about Hogwarts closing and the Chamber of Secrets parallel, which is thematically resonant.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Hagrid accompanies Harry to King's Cross / Diagon Alley escort
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book opens the Hogwarts year with Hagrid proudly escorting Harry through Diagon Alley, chest thrown out, thumbs in pockets, telling Tom the innkeeper 'Hogwarts business' in an self-importantly officious manner, standing guard outside Madam Malkin's, and reassuring Mrs. Weasley about the Malfoys in an unconcerned way that makes Harry, Ron and Hermione exchange knowing looks. It establishes Hagrid as trusted, proud, slightly bumbling security — and his pride at being chosen over Aurors by Dumbledore is explicit and touching.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This scene does not appear in the film corpus. The Diagon Alley sequence and Hagrid's escort role are entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: While the escort scene is not structurally critical, it provides important early-book characterisation: Hagrid's pride in Dumbledore's trust, his benign ineffectiveness as security (the trio slip away under the Invisibility Cloak while he hums obliviously), and his warm relationship with the Weasley family. Its absence means the film's Hagrid arrives in the story without this grounding, warm, slightly comedic reestablishment of who he is at the start of the sixth year.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 (INT. SITTING ROOM/KITCHEN - NIGHT) - Hagrid's comic interjection during the betrayal discussion
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, when suspicion falls on who betrayed the Order, Hagrid is not singled out for comic relief. Harry privately reflects on Hagrid's past mistake (giving Voldemort information for a dragon's egg) but defends him implicitly through his general statement of trust. Hagrid's vulnerability and the weight of potential suspicion is handled with emotional gravity; Harry's internal recognition that Hagrid was once tricked is a quiet, empathetic beat.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, when Arthur raises the question of betrayal and eyes shift, Hagrid launches into a prolonged, rambling, bumbling monologue ('I'd wager me life it wasn' none of you lot... Talk in me sleep on occasion... mostly gibberish... besides I'd cut me tongue out...') that plays as pure comic relief, making him look ridiculous and self-incriminating through buffoonery. The scene ends with everyone smiling at him as if he is a lovable fool.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book handles this moment with restraint and emotional intelligence — Harry privately notices the irony of Hagrid's past mistake but says nothing, choosing instead to issue a blanket statement of trust. The film converts this into a slapstick monologue that reduces Hagrid to a comic grotesque who inadvertently makes himself look guilty. His dignity in a tense, grief-laden scene is sacrificed for a laugh, undermining the emotional register of the whole sequence.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 (Film Scene 1, INT. SITTING ROOM/KITCHEN) - Hagrid's greeting on arrival
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Hagrid's arrival is described with physical presence and warmth ('All righ', Harry? Ready fer the off?'). He is presented as one of many but with the specific emotional resonance of being the one who brought Harry into the wizarding world — the motorbike moment and his 'An' the last time yeh was on it, Harry, I could fit yeh in one hand!' line convey deep affection and history. He is emotionally grounded and purposeful.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, Hagrid's arrival is staged as a slightly comedic beat — he yanks a small twittering bird from his beard ('Yeah, he's ruddy gorgeous. What say we get undercover before someone murders him'). While not severely damaging, this replaces genuine emotional warmth with a quirky gag, and his first words are a deflecting wisecrack rather than a term of affection toward Harry.
damaging_scenes.explanation: A minor but symptomatic shift: the film reaches for a comic quirk (bird in beard) rather than letting Hagrid's affection for Harry anchor his introduction to this high-stakes scene. The book's version carries emotional weight about their shared history; the film's version is a throwaway gag.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 9 (EXT. THE BURROW - NIGHT) - Hagrid's arrival at the Burrow and brandy request
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Hagrid arrives at the Burrow having survived a harrowing ordeal, collapses on landing, climbs laboriously to his feet, and asks for brandy 'a little shakily' — the shakiness conveying genuine trauma and vulnerability.
